items.title: This cocktail lounge was made almost entirely from USM modules
items.text: This cocktail lounge was made almost entirely from USM modules Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Josh Greenspan creates New York cocktail lounge almost entirely with USM modules Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ellen Eberhardt | 8 October 2026 Restaurateur Josh Greenspan and furniture company USM have created VV's Cocktail Room in Manhattan, a small space wrapped almost entirely in Steel Blue USM Haller modular shelving and informed by Greenspan's visits to Japan and Hong Kong . Named after Greenspan 's daughter Vivienne, VV's Cocktail Room (VV's) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. Josh Greenspan and USM have completed Manhattan cocktail bar VV's Cocktail Room The project stems from Greenspan's ongoing conversations with USM, which frequently collaborates with designers to outfit spaces and create installations from the flexible panelling system. "I started imagining something a little wild – a space built entirely from the USM system, pushing its modularity in unexpected ways," Greenspan told Dezeen. "I'm thrilled that the USM team embraced the idea and came along for the ride." The space is wrapped in a dark blue USM Haller System Visitors to the bar pass a glass block wall partition to enter the space. Inside, navy blue USM panels form the walls that surround the space and wrap behind the bar, where they jut out into shelving. A dark walnut wood was used for the bar top and tables, which is offset by bar seats upholstered in a burgundy fabric and banquette seating built by Greenspan's father, Michael Greenspan, covered in a similar hue. Read: Norwegian designers use reclaimed materials to customise USM Haller furniture Other details include a wavy pendant light by New York lighting studio Studio Kawabi that spans the length of the bar and a painting by Japanese artist Keita Morimoto affixed to the back wall. The space was informed by the "visual language" of Tokyo and Hong Kong, according to the team, and aims for the futuristic aesthetic between the 1960s and 1990s of the two metropolises. The panels expand into shelves behind the bar Greenspan worked with USM's director of architectural development, Ian Mutschelkanus, to create an interior where the USM Haller System serves as "the architectural framework of the space" rather than simply being inserted. "Rather than furnishing the interiors, USM defines them," said the team. "Each composition of the modular system demonstrates its remarkable versatility beyond furniture and into the realm of spatial design." It was informed by the "futuristic aesthetic" of Tokyo and Hong Kong between the 1960s and 1990s Greenspan partnered with James Beard Award-winning bartender Neal Bodenheimer and longtime friend Vincent Favela for the omakase cocktail program, while his mother, five-time James Beard Award winner Dorie Greenspan , created a bar snack menu. Past spaces that used USM panels for walls include retail space for Coperni in Paris . Other recently completed bars in New York include Odd Ball by House Under Magic and a second Brooklyn location for concept shop and wine bar Million Goods designed by Gjergji Shkurti . items.title: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum hides "in plain sight"
items.text: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum hides "in plain sight" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 18 July 2026 Architecture studio OMA has designed a "jewel box" restaurant clad in cork inside its recently completed extension to the New Museum in Manhattan. All-day bar and restaurant Oberon has opened a few months after the expansion, which OMA New York completed adjacent to the original SANAA-designed building. Oberon appears as a metallic box within the ground-floor lobby of the expanded New Museum Sitting adjacent to the lobby, in the expansion's ground floor, the 2,500-square-foot (230-square-metre) restaurant appears as a metallic box with a single horizontal band of frosted glass wrapping its exterior, hinting at what's inside. It was clad in cork that was then painted a silver colour, blending it into the industrial materials of the museum s[ace "'Hidden-in-plain-sight,' the restaurant resembles a jewel box or an inverted white cube gallery," said OMA. The restaurant can be entered from the museum lobby or a separate entrance on Freemans Alley The studio's first restaurant design in the US, Oberon is accessible directly from the museum lobby as well as a separate, speakeasy-style entrance from Freeman Alley. "We imagined the restaurant both as part of, and independent from the museum," said OMA New York partner Shohei Shigematsu. "Conceived as a freestanding box inserted into the ground-floor lobby, it will be accessible from the building's front and back, day to night." The moody, cavernous restaurant interior contrasts the bright industrial museum The interior's moody, cavernous aesthetic is a stark contrast to the museum's industrial concrete and metal lobby and galleries. "Inside, a large dining room and fixed pockets of seating will offer space to gather or retreat," said Shigematsu. "Organic, tactile material finishes complementing the museum's polished lightness, will introduce a warm and comforting environment that eases people in and invites them to stay." Booth seating and ceilings are made entirely from black expanded cork, while pendant lights are by Minjae Kim Over the central dining area, filled with freestanding wooden tables and chairs, the cork ceiling is carved away to create an elongated dome ringed with cove lighting. Around the restaurant perimeter, each booth sits below its own scooped metallic-coated ceiling element, from which a single pendant lamp by Minjae Kim descends to illuminate the tabletops. An interactive digital artwork by Ian Cheng is displayed behind the bar Tropical plants fill the open tops of the booths, casting silhouettes and shadows on the frosted glass that can be subtly traced from outside. Both the booth seats and the ceiling are formed entirely from black expanded cork, creating a homogenous appearance throughout the compact space. Read: OMA completes "highly connected, but highly individual" expansion of New York's New Museum "The restaurant uses a novel sustainable material which gives a rich softness counter to the museum's white box galleries," said project architect Jake Forster. "Produced in blocks by heating cork offcuts to a high temperature, the cork self-bonds by its natural resins creating an innovative material that can be cut and shaped." A horizontal band of frosted glass breaks up the metallic box-like exterior "A product mainly used for insulation – we have embraced its qualities, carving an intimate and hidden cavern, a new communal space, embedded within the museum," he added. An interactive digital artwork by Ian Cheng is displayed behind the bar, which is bookended by metal-grate partitions connected by a reflective ceiling. The restaurant has opened following the completion of the New Museum expansion earlier this year Elsewhere in the city, Office of Tangible Space recently renovated the interiors of the Brooklyn Museum Cafe , while other new restaurants include a Japanese-influenced spot next to the Stonewall Inn and the revamped dining venues at The Edge . OMA other recent news includes the completion of the pyramidal Hangzhou Prism in China and the creation an incubator for mushroom production at Fundación Casa Wabi in Mexico. The photography is by Alex Fradkin . items.text: Peak with Priceless restaurant revamped at The Edge in New York Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats New York's art deco icons inform revamped restaurant at The Edge Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 11 June 2026 Design studio Journey and Tao Hospitality Group have refreshed the interiors of dining venues at The Edge , the triangular observation deck at New York's Hudson Yards . The team has completely redesigned Peak with Priceless , the restaurant located on the 101th floor of the KPF-designed 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper. The interiors of Peak by Priceless have been redesigned so every seat has an uninterrupted skyline view The overhaul also includes the addition of Avenue Sky Lounge – a revival of the popular Avenue nightclub in Chelsea, which shuttered in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and never reopened. Susan Nugraha, Tao Group Hospitality 's SVP of design and development, worked closely on the project with experiential design group Journey . Custom tiered lighting nods to art deco skyscrapers such as the Empire State Building Both hospitality concepts draw design influences from the Manhattan skyline visible through the wraparound, floor-to-ceiling windows. "The inspiration behind Peak and Avenue was always New York itself, its energy, glamour and unmistakable sense of occasion," said Journey managing director David Taglione. "Suspended above the city with the skyline as its stage, we wanted to create a hospitality experience that feels both elevated and deeply connected to the rhythm of New York." Soft blue and warm brown suede covers the booth seating References to art deco structures such as the Empire State Building and Rockefeller Center can be spied in tall, tiered lamps, customised to softly illuminate both Peak and Avenue spaces. "Every design decision, from the rich materiality to the layered seating and subtle Art Deco references, was shaped to frame the view while creating a space with its own distinct sense of presence," said Taglione. Read: Edge sky deck protrudes from supertall Hudson Yards skyscraper At Peak, stepped booths are oriented towards the views, while smaller tables run along the windows – ensuring every seat has an unbroken sightline. Soft blue and warm brown suede upholster the curved seat backs, with wavy patterns echoed in partitions that run along the back of the dining space Avenue Sky Lounge (also main image) continues the same colour palette A similar colour palette appears across Avenue Sky Lounge , which can be divided into more intimate spaces by coffee-hued curtains that follow arched ceiling features. Lacquered wood panelling surrounds the bar, where more geometric shapes in the stone counters and liquor display cases again nod to art deco. "Our vision was a design that is both timeless and of the moment, seamlessly adapting to any time of day or occasion," said Nugraha. Lacquered wood panelling and geometric details around the bar again nod to the city's art deco icons The revamp at The Edge will also see the return of Marquee Skydeck , a series of events that include DJ sets and performances on the platform that at 1,100 feet (335 metres) above street level is currently the highest observation deck in the western hemisphere. Other sky-high hospitality venues in New York City include Manhatta , a Woods Bagot-designed restaurant atop 28 Liberty in the Financial District. The photography is courtesy of Tao Group Hospitality. items.text: Surrane Design designs Hommali restuarant in New York Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ellen Eberhardt | 4 September 2026 New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central "courtyard" space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house. Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn "Benz" Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee "Air" Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak "Picha" Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene. Surrane Design has completed a Thai restaurant in the West Village The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display. Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok's Chatuchak Weekend Market. It brings together a rich assortment of textures and colours informed by Thailand According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant. "The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice," said the team. Personal items from the ownership team line a partition It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country. Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet. Stairs lead to a mezzanine with additional seating Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces. Personal items from the ownership team, such as vintage Thai cookbooks from the late 1960s and early 1970s and other objects "one would expect to find in a living room" line the shelves. Small bamboo sculptures by Thai artist Korakot Aromdee are also peppered throughout the space. Read: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight" Wood-lined stairs lead to the mezzanine above, which contains additional seating concealed behind a frosted glass railing. A large skylight hangs above the space and sits over a large dining table. Banquets and an off-white white wallpaper embossed with 3D-printed plants also line the space. Like below, a curtain can be drawn across the length of the space to provide additional separation. A large skylight hangs above the space Hommali will serve contemporary takes on traditional Thai dishes created under Benz, such as a seafood cocktail with razor clams imbued with the hot and sour notes of tom yum and the Tomato, "a michelada-meets-spritz with a Singaporean rice wine base accompanied by a Thai chile tincture." Surrane Design is an independent design studio based in Brooklyn by partners Bud Nitaya and Yoon Her. items.title: Kimpton Ashbel hotel evokes elegance of New York townhouses
items.text: Kimpton Ashbel hotel evokes elegance of New York townhouses Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Busta Studio evokes the elegance of New York townhouses for Kimpton Ashbel hotel Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Cajsa Carlson | 14 August 2026 Interior design practice Busta Studio has filled the Kimpton Ashbel hotel on Park Avenue with art and objects intended to make it feel like "a warm, elegantly curated home". Located in a 1928 beaux-arts building on New York City's famous Park Avenue, Kimpton Ashbel was designed to feel like a private residence. A neutral colour palette is juxtaposed with jewel tones at Kimpton Ashbel "Park Avenue is one of New York City's most iconic streets, instantly evoking the elegance of its heritage townhouses," Busta Studio founder Anna Busta told Dezeen. "Drawing from this distinctive spirit, we envisioned a conceptual townhouse experience – welcoming guests into a warm, elegantly curated home." Artworks decorate both guestrooms and communal areas Anna and her husband Jonathan Busta, who run Busta Studio together, used hand-brushed blonde limed oak panelling and arches juxtaposed with Bianco Dolomiti and Pietra marbles to create the right feel for the interior. The studio also combined hand-cast bronze, glass, inlaid bronze and hand-cut mosaic stone with white plaster ceilings and mouldings for a deliberately simple yet elegant look. "The New York townhouse concept itself is an endless source of inspiration: a place where one lingers, surrounded by bespoke millwork, refined finishes, stylish furnishings, and a curated mix of art and collected objects that feel personal and storied," Jonathan Busta told Dezeen. The hotel was designed to feel like a home To create privacy from the bustle of Park Avenue, custom louvres were added at street level. Guests are welcomed by a custom inlaid mosaic featuring the hotel's KA initials when entering the lobby, which Busta Studio filled with specially commissioned artworks and decorative objects. Read: A-nrd designs Arthouse Glasgow hotel to "feel like it belongs to the city" "We curated the art collection to create a nice, easy vibe for the interior, with a mixture of graphics, original paintings, photography and sculpture," Anna Busta said. "All pieces are specifically commissioned for the space, and the overall collection has a simple but sophisticated guiding aesthetic," she continued. "We didn't want to provoke with art, but instead we simply embraced beauty." Designers Busta Studio added tactile materials and brass details The designers wanted to tie the communal spaces and guestrooms at Kimpton Ashbel together by using a coherent colour palette for the hotel, which focuses on calming neutral hues juxtaposed with jewel colours. "Jewel tones inject vibrancy into accent pieces like arch chairs, side stools, headboards, and art chairs, striking a harmonious balance between subtle and bold statements that add warmth and approachability to the space," Jonathan Busta said. Velvet and linen fabrics were used throughout the Park Avenue hotel To create a homely feeling, Busta Studio used velvets, linens, naturally tanned leathers and boucle fabrics. The studio said it hoped that the mix of tactile materials, refined finishes and well-considered artworks would create a feeling that is reminiscent of a well-designed home. "We believe the guest experience is enhanced by this intimate approach," Anna Busta concluded. Other hotels recently featured on Dezeen include a Glasgow hotel in a 19th-century townhouse and a Tokyo boutique hotel designed to feel like staying at the home of a friend . items.title: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
items.text: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 3 October 2026 Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York 's Rockefeller Plaza to emulate "a stateroom on an ocean liner". The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era's blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. "Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough," said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city's dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. "Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York's layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center," said INC's Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel's five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. Read: INC creates "gritty yet inviting" interiors for restaurant in The Spiral skyscraper On the roof, a bar references the dining rooms of Chinatown via a tomato-red counter framed by tiled portals, temple-like joinery and hand-painted lotus motifs. The Kimpton Era's guest rooms are designed like compact ship cabins, with each "berth" featuring full white-oak walls that integrate a bed, desk and storage into a single furniture element. White oak millwork integrates multiple furniture pieces in the guest rooms Neutral colour palettes are offset by jewel-toned fabrics and brass accents, while wet-room-style bathrooms are defined by frosted, blackened metal-framed sliding glass doors that conserve space. "[The Kimpton Era] is a self-contained voyage where guest rooms are like staterooms and lounges, and dining rooms unfold like the salons of a great ocean liner in a new expression of New York luxury," said INC's Louisa Revitte. Jewel-toned fabrics enliven the otherwise neutral rooms INC's previous hotel projects have included the 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with Marvel Architects, and the event spaces at the TWA Hotel inside Eero Saarinen's JFK Airport terminal. The studio – which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year – has also completed "gritty yet inviting" interiors for a restaurant in BIG's The Spiral skyscraper, and filled its own concrete-forward offices with eclectic furniture and plants. The photography is by Read McKendree . items.text: Formant Studio designs Nota restaurant in Mexico City Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Ben Dreith | 9 October 2026 Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence. Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. "The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity," Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. "The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language." The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Also in the tradition of the 20th-century modern architects, Formant Studio designed most of the furniture, from the black-stained oak tables to the steel bar stools and sleek metal sconces. The space was once a hacienda-style residence and its original columns were preserved and restored The majority of the dining room was clad in Mexican rosewood panels, which also form the custom banquettes upholstered in black Kvadrat textiles. Formant Studio said that the previous space defined how it organised the restaurant. Mexican rosewood covers the walls and forms banquette seating The current space still has ornate stone pillars that once framed an entrance portico. The team removed the paint from the pillars, turning them into a centrepiece of the main dining space. An entrance vestibule holds a host stand and a door leads to a metal spiral staircase painted in a rich brown. This staircase leads to a private dining room upstairs. Past the host stand, the main dining room opens up. Visitors walk into a front area with a large banquette and a seating bar that looks out of an operable window onto the street. The design was drawn from classic Chicago taverns "The shape of the existing space largely determined the furniture layout," said Valencia. "We used the longer walls to accommodate the built-in booths, establishing a clear spatial rhythm while keeping the central area flexible and allowing the dining room to adapt to different group sizes and configurations." Read: Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn Past the columns, the room has an array of tables arranged under the double-height ceiling. The rafters of the former space were painted white and a mezzanine from the private dining space juts out over a row of banquette seating. This mezzanine has a high boundary that provides privacy from below. At the back of the space is the bar, with a mirror backsplash and rosewood millwork above. Steel contrasts with wood and minimalist decor A sound system by Paxwave was installed in the space. The tablescapes were styled with sheer white cloths, which contrast with the stained-black chairs and the polished grey terrazzo flooring. The kitchen space sits under the private dining room and is hidden from the main space. More mirrors line the wall that divides the kitchen, while the windows opposite have metal grating. Street-facing windows bring light into the space, where mirrors were used to further diffuse the light Art and antiques were curated by Galería Córdoba . Formant Studio also designed its own studio in Mexico City , which it shares with photographer Fabián Martinez . Dezeen included Formant Studio in a list of notable Mexico designers earlier this year. The photography is by Fabián Martinez. items.title: Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar
items.text: Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Fabio Fantolino looks to 1960s offices for interior of retro Turin bar Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alice Laycock | 29 June 2026 Cantilever chairs , wood panelling and mirror -clad surfaces meet in Lève Office Bar, a Space Age-informed bar in Turin by Italian architect Fabio Fantolino . The venue is located in the centre of the Italian city and nods to the aesthetics and culture of workplaces built in post-war America. A stainless steel bar sets the tone upon entry The original building dates from the 1920s and before the intervention, it was divided into two distinct units: one contained a cafe, while the other housed a bookshop. It now functions as one cohesive interior subdivided into three spaces, all of which reference retro workplaces. Herringbone bricks give way to green resin flooring beyond The space aims to serve professionals working in the city centre over the course of a typical working day; hence the architect's decision to theme it around retro offices. "The 1960s were chosen as the reference period because they marked a time when offices were regarded as prestigious and carefully designed workplaces – the 'office bar' concept, on the other hand, reflects the way we work today," Fantolino told Dezeen. "It is conceived as a space that supports the everyday rhythm of contemporary office life, whether for breakfast, lunch, coffee breaks, or aperitivos, while also acknowledging that work can naturally extend into hospitality spaces." All the fittings and fixtures were selected according to 1960s aesthetics "The three areas reinterpret the concept of an open-plan office, each through a distinct design language," Fantolino continued. A monolithic stainless-steel bar dominates the initial interior upon entry. Its strong presence is bolstered by a red enamel wall panel mounted behind it. The ceiling beneath the mezzanine presents a mirrored alternative to conventional grid ceilings The effect is softened by a herringbone floor made up of sandy-coloured bricks, which gives way to a green resin floor at the threshold of the second space. Banquette seating upholstered in fawn-coloured leather runs along the far wall, accompanied by red-topped cafe tables and brown-and-chrome cantilever chairs. Read: Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar in London Seating for bar-goers sits within the double-height space, with more tucked beneath the mezzanine, where a lower ceiling clad in mirrored panels puts a chic spin on dropped ceilings common in offices. The upstairs mezzanine is where the office spaces are most closely mimicked, with cubicle-like segments created by high-backed, boucle-upholstered sofas placed back-to-back. The mezzanine was a preexisting architectural feature Partitions up here create intimacy for guests, rather than privacy for focused work, with the area making use of the preexisting mezzanine to create a cosy bolt-hole. "The mezzanine introduces office-style partition elements to create a more intimate and structured atmosphere," said Fantolino. Upstairs, high-backed sofas create segmented private zones The pendant lights on the mezzanine, as well as the sconces attached to the walls beneath and the illuminated panels integrated into the dropped ceiling, reinforce the 1960s aesthetic. The overall neutral colour palette is made more interesting by pops of green, red and mustard, as well as material contrast between flat enamel, shiny chrome and tactile leather. The overall warmth of the material and colour palette is contrasted by metallic elements "The intention was to evoke the feeling of stepping back into the 1960s, creating an immersive atmosphere that feels almost like entering a time machine while remaining fresh and contemporary," Fantolino concluded. Other distinctive bars published on Dezeen include a bar in Rome decorated with disembodied plaster limbs and a Hong Kong bar featuring a lime green interior studded with tiny lights . The photography is by Luca Argenton. Read more: Interiors Italy Bars Turin Fabio Fantolino Subscribe to our newsletters Your email address New! items.title: "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona bar
items.text: "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona bar Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats "Progressive spirit" of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona cocktail bar Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alyn Griffiths | 28 June 2026 Spanish designer Isern Serra has completed a speakeasy bar in Barcelona featuring multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton 's retro-futuristic 1960s installations. Focacha is the latest venue from hospitality specialist Grupo La Confitería, which tasked Serra 's studio with creating a space that pays tribute to an important period in the history of Barcelona's nightlife. Isern Serra has designed a Barcelona bar with multi-coloured modular furniture that evokes Verner Panton pieces The 1960s and early 1970s coincided with the heyday of Tuset Street where the bar is located, which became a hub for a group of young liberal professionals known in Barcelona art the "gauche divine". The cocktail bar was designed to evoke the futuristic styling that characterised this time and immerse guests in a multi-sensory environment defined by design, light and music. The bar is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria "I wanted visitors to feel enveloped by an environment with a strong artistic and emotional presence, capable of sparking curiosity and creating a sense of wonder from the very first moment," Serra told Dezeen. "More than designing a cocktail bar, the intention was to create a setting that evokes emotions, encourages contemplation and leaves a lasting impression on those who experience it, turning their visit into something truly memorable." Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop The speakeasy-style venue is hidden behind the facade of a traditional focacceria that has been serving Italian bread for 50 years. Visitors enter through a refrigerator inside the shop, which adds a sense of theatricality to the experience. The venue was divided into two spaces, the first of which is a bar that pays homage to Danish designer Panton's iconic Visiona installations. A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space A sequence of seven organically shaped modules ranging in colour from yellow to red surround the space, forming intimate niches for small groups along one side. On the other side of the space, a stainless-steel bar with rounded edges subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room. The fully carpeted ceiling and walls extend behind the bar, where rounded openings accommodate shelves displaying bottles. A stainless-steel bar subtly reflects the vibrant colours and movement within the room "We were inspired by Panton because his creative language perfectly reflects the optimistic, experimental and progressive spirit of the late 1960s and early 1970s," Serra pointed out. "The goal was not to recreate a retro aesthetic, but to capture the sense of freedom, creativity and innovation that defined that era." The DJ room was lined with curved banquettes A circular opening at the end of the bar leads into a DJ room designed to merge 1960s nostalgia with a dystopian vision of the future, resulting in a surreal, technology-led aesthetic. The room is lined with curved banquettes that evoke the era's psychedelic and modular interiors, while the domed ceiling and walls incorporate openings that allow dynamic lighting effects to transform the atmosphere within the space. Read: Interior of FUBA bakery in Madrid explores "dialogue between the ancestral and futuristic" Mirrored walls create the illusion of more space, while lighting fixtures including the Panton-designed Flowerpot VP2 and Panthella lamps contribute to a carefully curated atmosphere. According to Serra, the interior's complex curves demanded a sculptural construction approach that meant elements were not fully defined from the outset and evolved as different solutions were tested using mock-ups and full-scale prototypes. Isern Serra said that the interior's complex curves demanded a sculptural construction "Rather than building conventional architectural elements," he said, "we were shaping volumes and forms to create a fluid and immersive spatial experience, where every curve contributed to reinforcing the overall atmosphere of the project." Serra's studio is based in the Poblenou neighbourhood of Barcelona, in a space he designed to embody the practice's values and provide an inspirational working environment. The architect is known for combining contemporary, vibrant and essential forms with Mediterranean influences. Previous projects include a gallery-like apartment renovation and a bakery featuring cave-like walls . items.title: Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar
items.text: Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Velvet walls and floors "retain the imprint of bodies" at Dive bar in London Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Alyn Griffiths | 18 June 2026 Design studio Golem has completed a subterranean cocktail bar in central London featuring a glossy counter and tactile booths entirely covered in soft red velvet. Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive "Dive's experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests," explained Golem founder Ariel André. "The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills." "Wear and tear is part of the architecture," he added. "Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies." The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive's owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains "the imprint of bodies" "The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus," André explained. A dark corridor leads to the steps that descend into the richer, more tactile lounge space. This area was designed to facilitate moments of interaction between guests, while also offering cosy corners for private conversations. Structural arches supporting the street above contain flexible seating areas that can be configured to suit various social scenarios. Built-in benches lining the niches are covered with loose cushions that can be repositioned as required. "The upholstery is conceived to be appropriated by guests," André pointed out. "Bodies shape the furniture, not the other way around." "When unoccupied, the seating still carries the imprint of previous guests, holding the evening in a suspended time and space." Golem aimed to create cosy corners for private conversations One of the arches known as the "fun room" is covered from floor to ceiling in lush carpet, allowing its U-shaped layout to be used for anything from lounging to dancing. Golem created quart-de-lune tables specially for the project, which can be used individually by couples sitting side by side, or combined in sets of two or four to comfortably seat up to eight guests. The main bar features contrasting smooth, glossy finishes The lounge also functions as a listening room, with the choice of absorbent and reflective surfaces helping to create a tailored acoustic environment. A dedicated DJ booth is positioned next to bespoke shelves housing the owner's extensive vinyl collection. The mixing desk is height adjustable to allow for seated or standing performance. A one-way mirror conceals the bathroom At the centre of the bar, the non-gendered bathrooms are arranged around a banquette where guests can sit and chat. A one-way mirror conceals this space from the outside while providing a glimpse back into the lounge. André founded his Paris-based studio in 2021, working across the worlds of architecture, art and design. Previous Golem projects include a modular furniture system made of hundreds of squishy balls , which was used to create a conversation pit in a Brussels apartment. items.title: Curtains create cosy corners in listening bar Upstairs at Hausu
items.text: Curtains create cosy corners in listening bar Upstairs at Hausu Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Curtains create cosy corners in Peckham listening bar Upstairs at Hausu Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Natasha Levy | 11 May 2026 Wool and sheer voile curtains envelop this intimate listening bar in south London designed by artist Eva Gold, drawing on references including David Lynch 's Twin Peaks series and a modernist Mies van der Rohe installation. Upstairs at Hausu is located directly above Hausu restaurant, which serves an array of Asian-inspired small plates to the soundtrack of jazz, soul and electronic vinyl . The bar is one floor up from Peckham's Hausu restaurant The newly added bar similarly plays music records but also hosts an array of DJs and serves a robust selection of cocktails that riff on the food offered downstairs. When designer and artist Eva Gold was put in charge of the bar's interiors, television and cinema ended up being key points of reference – fitting given that Hausu was named after a 1977 Japanese horror-comedy film. Brown woollen curtains were hung around the edge of the room Her main inspiration was The Red Room from director David Lynch's cult series Twin Peaks, a surreal, multidimensional space engulfed by crimson curtains. Gold was also influenced by The Velvet and Silk Cafe , an installation created by designer Lilly Reich and architect Mies van der Rohe for a fashion exhibition in 1927 that featured several curved "walls" and partitions made from swathes of fabric. Sheerer curtains act as dividers between tables "I wanted the cocktail bar to feel dark and intimate," Gold told Dezeen. "So I thought a lot about desire, and its connection to the unknown." "Both [The Red Room and The Velvet and Silk Cafe] utilise curtains, essentially playing with the idea of concealing or obscuring something." Read: Peckham Palais nightclub reopens with "layered and atmospheric" interior Upstairs at Hausu is framed by a series of different curtains. Heavy chocolate-coloured wool drapes run around the periphery of the space, complementing the deep-brown dado painted around the lower half of the bar's white walls. Sheer voile curtains were suspended between a few of the wooden tables, creating cosy pockets of seating; these can be drawn back to accommodate larger groups if needed. Music is fed through speakers that sit at different points throughout the room Speakers are dotted throughout the room to provide balanced, high-quality sound, with some mounted in the corners and larger models set on the floor. The space is softly illuminated by paper lanterns that dangle from the ceiling. Decoration was otherwise kept simple with potted plants and a slender metal shelf displaying vinyl covers. Vinyl covers are displayed on metal shelving Upstairs at Hausu isn't the only drinks spot to have recently landed in this corner of south London. Last month saw the reopening of nightclub Peckham Palais . After being closed for 15 years, the venue now has a "layered and atmospheric" interior featuring raspberry-red walls and leather banquettes. The photography is by Adam Firman . items.title: "Timeless futurism" defines Hong Kong bar by Studio Paolo Ferrari
items.text: "Timeless futurism" defines Hong Kong bar by Studio Paolo Ferrari Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats "Timeless futurism" defines Hong Kong cocktail bar Peridot by Studio Paolo Ferrari Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 15 April 2026 Over 20,000 tiny lights glow across this lime-green bar by Toronto-based Studio Paolo Ferrari , located at the top of Zaha Hadid Architects' The Henderson in Hong Kong. Peridot serves a menu of fermentation-forward, plant-based cocktails and fare to guests on the 38th floor of The Henderson building, which completed in 2024. At Peridot, thousands of tiny lights dot the curved walls and ceiling Studio Paolo Ferrari approached the space in a style its founder describes as "timeless futurism", and the result is a cocoon-like interior enveloped almost entirely in lime green. "We wanted the space to embody the energy and dynamism of Hong Kong, a space rooted in the elegance of the past, but propelled by possibility," said Ferrari. Green marble forms the service counter and a mirrored ceiling reflects the liquor bottle display behind The bar interior's continuously curved walls and ceiling are dotted with over 20,000 tiny lights that shine through protruding frosted acrylic cylinders. The effect of these pixel-like elements is akin to an exploded disco ball, and the surrealism is intensified by the all-green decor and its reflective surfaces. "There's a sense of infinite expansion, but it's deeply personal, abstract, yet strangely familiar," said Ferrari. A marble-lined passage leads to a hidden lounge Echoing the architecture, sculptural sinuous walls frame large windows that overlook the Hong Kong skyline, which guests can enjoy from curvaceous mohair-upholstered sofas and lounge chairs. The service counter sits within another framed arch, almost like a theatrical stage, and is made from green marble that extends across the adjacent walls and spills onto the floor. The effect of the tiny lights is even more impactful inside the windowless lounge A mirrored ceiling reflects the illuminated back bottle display and the cocktail servers preparing drinks in front. "Familiar forms are abstracted, noble materials are reframed, and the result is a space that invites both reflection and projection," Ferrari said. "This is Timeless Futurism: memory in dialogue with courageous invention." Curvaceous sofas are tucked into alcoves, and the lights reflect off stainless steel tables and the arched door frame Hidden behind the bar, accessed via a curved marble-lined corridor, is an intimate lounge area that can be closed off for private events. In this windowless space, the tiny lights create an even more dramatic effect as they envelop guests and reflect off the curvaceous chrome-finished doorway and tables. Read: Studio Paolo Ferrari designs Toronto restaurant as a "world unto itself" Facing the entrance to the lounge is a custom wine case, housed within a cylindrical volume and featuring scoop-like stainless-steel forms that each display a single bottle. "Each cantilevered holder is engineered, as much as it is sculpted, highlighting Ferrari's rigour in detail," said the Peridot team. Bespoke stainless-steel wine bottle holders fill a display case More dramatic green marble lines the bathrooms, where basins are carved into a monolithic rounded plinth and porthole-like mirrors are ringed in lights. "Every surface, object, and transition contributes to a holistic story that suspends disbelief, while remaining entirely grounded in craft," the team said. The green marble also covers the bathroom walls and floor, and forms a sculptural basin The Henderson was built on a site in Hong Kong’s Central district that cost $3 billion – the most expensive in the world to date – and its sculptural glass form is based on the bud of a Bauhinia, the city’s emblematic flower. Studio Paolo Ferrari’s previous hospitality projects range in scale from a cinematic Toronto restaurant , to the interiors of the mirrored orbs that form the Shebara Resort in Saudi Arabia. items.text: Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for Cassette Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Rachael Gilby | 12 October 2026 Design studio Gundry & Ducker has renovated the interiors of a Grade II-listed workshop for Cassette, a Parisian-style bistro that has recently opened in the heart of London 's West End. The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing. The design was informed by traditional Parisian bistros Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level. An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits. "Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town," Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen. "From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city." The studio chose a warm, neutral colour palette for the interior The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs. Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall "deliberately unfussy" interior. The design combines a mixture of dark woods with natural fabrics and stainless steel "We talked a lot about colour: summer park landscapes, Parisian bistros and wine," Gundry explained. "Tone too was really important; we needed colours that would dim well to help us create a low-level evening setting that feels warm; the key to which is controlling reflected light," he continued. The Grade II-listed interior has double-height ceilings and a large glass facade Taking cues from the surrounding theatre district, the studio installed a sophisticated sound system and a statement curtain with acoustic qualities that wraps around the main dining area. "We felt that we could explore the world of theatres given the restaurant's location in London's West End," Gundry said. Read: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant "By placing the curtain within gantry structures, they became theatre curtains and added some character to the space," he continued. "In this case, acoustics was as much part of the conversation as colour or operation. The curtains help to control reverb and talk about a softer acoustic." A statement curtain wraps around the top of the main dining room Cassette's owners, Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, sourced a selection of artworks from local markets and car boot sales to add pops of colour and personality into the space. Other restaurant interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Bétyle Studio's design for Parisian eatery Arcane 17 and the newly opened Skywalker Grill located in the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles . items.text: Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell" Magazine Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Follow: Architecture Interiors Design Technology Series Features Interviews Opinion News Lookbooks Talks Videos Podcasts About Comments Newsletters Preferences Submit a story Advertise Privacy notice Contact Dezeen Magazine dezeen-logo dezeen-logo Next story clear Search --> --> Follow: Awards Jobs Events Guide Showroom School Shows Courses Competitions Series Interviews Opinion Talks Videos Newsletters Podcasts Magazine Architecture Interiors Design Technology --> Search results: Read more: Posts: --> Refine your search: Cats Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell" Share: Prefer Dezeen on Google Dan Howarth | 1 August 2026 Japanese minimalism has informed the interiors of this light-filled Italian restaurant in Montreal , designed by locally based Ivy Studio with its first in-house designed chairs. Located on the ground level of a Downtown high-rise residential tower, Minnibar utilises the 20-foot (6-metre) ceilings, corner aspect and almost square floor plan to its advantage. At the entrance to Minnibar, a pale stone-clad cafe counter drops in height to become an omakase-style ledge Ivy Studio left the building's structure entirely visible, and only added elements where functionally necessary – using the principles of Japanese minimalism as a guide. "Minnibar embraces its raw shell," said the studio. "Exposed base-building elements – including the naturally sealed concrete floor, formidable concrete columns, walls, and the ceiling slab – are left untouched." A slender black ledge along the windows provides space for dining The kitchen, bar and pizza counter are housed within an enclosed central core, allowing the cafe and restaurant spaces to flow openly around the perimeter. Morning patrons have easy access from the entrance to the cafe counter, which is clad in monolithic, cream-colored stone with a leather finish. Triangular shapes can be spotted in the wall-mounted lighting and millwork details As it continues into the space, the counter drops in height and is replaced with an omakase-style ledge crafted from white oak. Opposite, a black shelf runs along the windows to provide additional bar dining space, accompanied by circular white stools. The main dining area is arranged symmetrically around glowing wall-mounted artwork "The design employs a strict monochromatic palette, playing with off-white and grey shades punctuated by sharp black integrations," said Ivy Studio. "To give the minimalist aesthetic a profound sense of depth, the design introduces subtle, highly tactile finishes: hand-plastered walls, heavily textured stones, opaque stained wood grains, and translucent textiles." A custom stainless steel DJ booth sits at the apex of sight lines in two directions The main dining space features freestanding black tables for flexibility, which are typically arranged in a symmetrical layout around an adjustable glowing artwork on the back wall. Several custom furnishings, which represent "a study in contrast and craftsmanship," are installed throughout the restaurant. A largely monochromatic palette evokes a Japanese minimalist aesthetic These include Ivy Studio's first in-house designed chair, which features softly curved legs and a delicate backrest – all crafted from ash wood and stained soft yellow. The sculptural, stainless steel DJ booth was created in collaboration with local shop Procedures Industries and is equipped with built-in vinyl players. Read: Ivy Studio designs "bold and glamorous" Montreal restaurant Triangular details recur throughout, including in the stainless steel bar counter footrest, windows into the wine cellar, wall-mounted light fixtures and millwork. Rice-paper screens help to shade the interiors from bright sunlight and also form acoustic buffers across the ceiling. The omakase-style bar and accompanying chairs are crafted from white oak "Minnibar successfully harmonises the gritty, raw shell of downtown Montreal's urban architecture with the refined, atmospheric principles of Japanese minimalism," said the studio. "By contrasting heavy, exposed concrete with custom monolithic furniture, dynamic lighting, and an uncompromising dedication to sound and culinary craft, the space transcends the traditional restaurant model to offer a truly immersive, day-to-night destination." The restaurant features Ivy Studio's first chair designed in-house Ivy Studio has completed multiple restaurants across Montreal, including the "bold and glamorous" Limousine , the marble-filled Hayat , and Piatti , which was resurrected after a fire. The firm's portfolio also includes an indoor golf club , an ad agency in a converted bank and a creative hub with a "work in progress" aesthetic . The photography is by Alex Lesage . Sous Sous 4.7 · French - American · $$$ Los Angeles Book Now Published: Oct. 9, 2026 New hotels in Silver Lake only come along once in a decade (if that), and rarer still are hotels located inside former churches. Enter Hotel Lucile : the brand-new boutique hotel inside a restored 1930s-era church debuted last month after six years of renovations, and with it, comes a new restaurant called Sous Sous located inside the church’s former nave. Casetta Group is behind the entire project, the same hospitality team who brought you hotels like Malibu’s Surfrider and Palm Springs’ Casa Cody. For Sous Sous, they tapped veteran chef Patrick Costa, chef/owner of Downtown’s focaccia-pizza joint, De La Nonna . Here, he departs from Italian food, instead diving into his roots in both the American Southeast and Southern France, using seafood to connect the culinary dots. Josephine 4.4 · French-Italian · $ Silver Lake Book Now Published: Oct. 16, 2026 After 20 years cooking in some of the country’s most storied kitchens, there’s something about opening a restaurant with your best childhood friend that just feels like coming home. After opening inside a vintage Craftsman house in Silver Lake earlier this summer, Josephine draws from the personal nostalgia of two California natives, including family recipes reimagined, and nods to their 1990s childhood bedrooms. The buzzy new restaurant looks like equal parts dive bar and rustic Tahoe cabin, but feels like nonna’s house, with hearty slow-cooked dishes and pastas that lean heavily into French and Italian influences. After a shared childhood playing hockey together in San Jose, Anthony Dragotto and Marco Gagliardi worked in very different fields throughout most of their twenties and thirties. Gagliardi sharpened his culinary chops at spots like Zahav , Vetri Cucina, and High Street on Hudson in Philadelphia, as well as Bon Delire in San Francisco, while Dragotto worked in various industries, including tech sales, back in California. It wasn’t until these two old friends reunited at the Oasis concert in Pasadena that they started cooking up the idea for Josephine. “We just kept talking about it, joking about it, drinking over it, and then we decided: ‘All right, screw it, let’s start a restaurant,” Gagliardi says. More than a century later, Hoshino Resorts has transformed the former prison into Hoshinoya Nara Prison , , a 48-suite luxury hotel that preserves the building’s distinctive architecture while introducing an entirely new purpose. Photography courtesy of Hoshino Resorts Though the converted prison-hotel model isn’t anything new, Hoshinoya Nara Prison approaches adaptive reuse as an exercise in cultural preservation. With support from conservation specialists at Yasui Architects & Engineers , lead architect Rie Azuma ( Azuma Environmental Architectural Research Institute ) carried out a considered renovation that’s both deeply respectful of the site’s history and resolutely contemporary. Photography courtesy of Hoshino Resorts The Nara Prison complex relies on the conventional Haviland System—a radial layout in which five wings extend from a central guardhouse. Rather than masking this rigid institutional typology, Azuma and her team embraced its structural geometry, preserving the original circulation routes and emphasizing the architectural rhythm of the long corridors and brick arches. Photography courtesy of Hoshino Resorts “We aim to preserve the memory of how [Japanese people] of the time engaged with unfamiliar Western culture, while creating a space where modern guests can enjoy a comfortable stay,” Azuma explains. Despite this rigid geometry, the resulting interiors balance the building’s imposing architecture with the warmth and comfort expected of a contemporary hotel. A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designed Onuki restaurant. Back in 2024 we asked the Greek design studio Objects of Common Interest to compile their 10 favorite modernist buildings from around the country . The Hilton in Athens was not one of them, but it easily could have been; Hiltons these days may not be the first thing you think of when you think “design hotel,” but this one was built in 1963 by prominent Greek architects Prokopis Vassiliadis, Emmanouil Vourekas, and Spyros Staikos, who hired artist Yiannis Moralis to adorn its front facade with an iconic, very midcentury-coded display of Greek hospitality-themed engravings. Add to that its landmark 82-foot pool, and the modernist building was long venerated both as a hotel and a piece of cultural history. Now, having undergone a four-year restoration and renovation, it has reopened to much fanfare as Conrad Athens the Ilisian , its 278 guest rooms and public spaces reimagined by AvroKo — with a restaurant by Yabu Pushelberg . While the new interiors definitely have that luxury-corporate-hotel vibe in some areas, there are lots of nice midcentury touches — both original and inspired by the original. The former are concentrated in the hotel lobby , where bronze snail-shaped fountains from the original pool, by Moralis and Bouba Lyberaki, have been repositioned into a long water feature that runs down the center of the space. At one end is a fully restored 1963 ceramic mural that Moralis created for the Hilton’s rooftop Galaxy Bar. The hotel’s suites feature elements like the Praying Mantis lamp that Francois Rispal designed in 1950, plus a newly created wood relief wall mural, pictured above, that clearly pays homage to the era.
